text:
Recent work supports aligning collaborative IDs with text while controlling semantic noise. [ASIF (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3589335.3648308) uses contrastive ID–side-information alignment and orthogonal decomposition to extract shared information. [DenseRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18442) learns a projection from pretrained content embeddings into the ID space; its analysis attributes gains mainly to sequence representations containing unseen items. Neither establishes that a randomly initialized text encoder will improve GRU4Rec. An older, relevant precedent, [Ask the GRU](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02116), trains a GRU text encoder end-to-end through collaborative recommendation and auxiliary metadata prediction, although it is not the required sequential GRU4Rec architecture.

Frequency conditioning has adjacent support: [FAAM-SR (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2026.123580) incorporates behavioral frequency into learned gates and recurrent updates, but does not establish frequency-aware text–ID fusion. A reasonable experimental hypothesis is one GRU4Rec with a jointly trained token-pooling encoder, projected title/description features, and a gate conditioned on training-only log item count and text availability. Add a small same-item ID–text contrastive loss alongside next-item training; mask duplicate-item negatives. These are proposed adaptations, not published guarantees.

Controls should distinguish item-specific transfer from broad lexical association: ID-only; fusion without alignment; fixed versus frequency-conditioned gates; title-only versus title-plus-description; and item-text shuffling within training-frequency bins, preserving each document’s vocabulary and length. Inspect validation HR@10 by target-frequency bin, gate values, and text-embedding similarity/collapse. Retain a single jointly trained checkpoint per category; compare variants through separate trials, never score fusion.
